name: Vicks VapoRub on the chest, feet and nose
what_people_do: Rub Vicks on the chest, back, soles of the feet (under socks) or under the nose for colds, coughs and asthma, including on children.
why_they_say_it_works: The menthol "opens the chest"; rubbing the feet is believed to pull the cold down.

documented_by.source: Reznik M et al 2004, J Altern Complement Med, PMID 15674007
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Bronx high school, 165 adolescents with asthma: 11% used rubbing ointments as first treatment for their last attack; ethnicity of this group not given in the abstract.

documented_by.source: Esguerra CR et al 2025, J Pediatr Nurs, PMID 41067089
documented_by.quote_or_summary: New York City adolescents with uncontrolled asthma (Hispanic/Latinx and Black, n=212): Vicks VapoRub was one of the surveyed beliefs; solely Hispanic/Latinx youth had higher odds of believing it helps than youth identifying as both Hispanic and Black; no Black-only prevalence in the abstract.

evidence.tested: Vapor rub on chest and neck at bedtime vs petrolatum vs nothing
evidence.population: 138 US children aged 2 to 11 (ethnicity not stated)
evidence.finding: Vapor rub scored best for cough, congestion and sleep, ahead of petrolatum and no treatment; irritant side effects more common with the rub.

source.name: Paul IM et al 2010, Pediatrics, PMID 21059712 (vapor rub vs petrolatum vs nothing)

headline_tier_note: Tier is for chest and neck rub in children; foot rub untested.
harm_note: Tested only in children aged 2 to 11; more irritation than petrolatum. Not tested in babies under two. The "feet" version has no source I opened.
gaps: Regional prevalence among Caribbean, African and Black British families not found.
A "Vicks on the feet" mechanism or trial not found.
